title: ISRO Rocket Woman Nandini Harinath's Saree Lands at the Smithsonian
excerpt: The red block-printed saree worn during India's Mars Orbiter Mission now sits among Apollo capsules and lunar rovers in Washington, D.C.
body:
A red and blue block-printed saree has joined the ranks of spacesuits and moon rocks at the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum in Washington, D.C. The garment belongs to Nandini Harinath, one of ISRO's celebrated "rocket women," who wore it on the day India's Mars Orbiter Mission — Mangalyaan — departed Earth's gravitational pull in 2013.

From Sriharikota to the National Mall:

Harinath served as deputy operations director for Mangalyaan, the mission that made India the first Asian nation and the fourth space agency worldwide to reach Martian orbit. Completed at a cost of roughly $74 million — less than the budget of the Hollywood film Gravity — the mission became a global symbol of frugal engineering excellence. The saree, worn during one of the mission's most critical phases, has now been selected by the Smithsonian's curators as an artifact representing India's growing role in space exploration.

Harinath, born to a mathematics teacher and an engineer, joined ISRO after completing her postgraduate engineering degree and has contributed to more than 14 missions over a career spanning two decades. She has spoken publicly about being inspired by Star Trek and Apollo 13 as a child — a fitting origin story for someone whose professional life now literally occupies the same museum halls as the Apollo program's relics.

Why It Resonates Across the Diaspora:

For the 4.4 million Indian-Americans in the United States, many of whom pass the Air and Space Museum on school trips and weekend outings, the display carries a particular charge. It is not a spacecraft or a sensor package on exhibit — it is a saree, an everyday garment transformed into a symbol of scientific ambition. The juxtaposition is deliberate: curators have placed it alongside high-tech hardware to underscore that breakthroughs emerge from people, not just machines.

The display also arrives at a moment when representation of South Asians in STEM leadership is under active discussion in American universities and workplaces. Harinath's story — a woman who rose through ISRO's ranks in an era when female engineers were scarce — offers a concrete, museum-certified counter to lingering stereotypes.

What to Watch:

The Smithsonian has not announced how long the saree will remain on display, but the museum's history suggests high-profile acquisitions tend to become permanent fixtures. ISRO, meanwhile, continues to expand its mission portfolio, with the Gaganyaan crewed spaceflight program next on the horizon — meaning more artifacts may eventually follow Harinath's saree across the ocean.
